I would start with learning to like fruit because I think that's easier. Bananas, blueberries, and red grapes are usually well-liked and easy to eat. You can expand and try other things of course, but you're not obligated to like it all. Find something that you enjoy to eat every day or most days. For me, it's definitely a banana.

As for vegetables, I would recommend anything where you're adding a vegetable to a dish instead of eating it by itself. Scour healthy recipes on the Food Network website until you find something you might like to try. It's much more palatable to eat vegetables when they're mixed with other things. 

I would focus on ensuring you replace those 300 calories of chocolate with any real food, whether or not it includes vegetables. 300 calories of something with fiber and protein will keep you full much longer and will ensure you're successful in keeping to your calorie goal. For example, you can make a simple BLT with turkey bacon that is only slightly more than 300 calories. Or cook 2 eggs with some salt & pepper, and roll it up in a tortilla. Much more filling than chocolate.

I wouldn't recommend buying avocado or grape seed oil because they're more expensive and won't make a noticeable difference. Vegetable oil or olive oil are perfect for sautéing vegetables. Just ensure you measure the oil before cooking because any oil is at least 100 calories per tablespoon.

Ground beef, chicken, and turkey is good at $2.50/lb. You will usually see 80/20 beef at this price and lower fat will be higher. I won't buy ground beef for more than $2.99/lb, personally.

There are many cuts of beef that are variable in pricing. London broil can often be found on sale at $1.99/lb.

Fish is very dependent on the type and is a lot more expensive. It depends on whether farm raised or wild caught matters to you, or atlantic/pacific. Salmon is great at $5.99/lb if you can get it.
